units.translation: 495-99. Peleus advises that after the death of Apsyrtus they sail against the remaining Colchians, saying that at dawn, having seen what was done, they will pursue us, not with one accord.
505. <Electrida:> this Electris is near the river Eridanus.

507-21. The Colchians, when the Argo set sail, did not return for fear of Aeetes, but some of them settled where Apsyrtus was treacherously slain, with the people called Apsyrtians after him, and others in Illyria, where the Encheleis are around the Ceraunian mountains.
524. Hylleans: a people around Illyria, named from Hyllus, son of Heracles and Melite.
531. hierēn peusome<nos>: inquiry, about to ask an oracle from Apollo.
532-33. hopēi chthonos hidryth<eien>: the Hylleans, having received
a tripod from Jason as a reward for showing the way, hid it under the ground, since the oracle commanded that wherever the tripod should be, the city would be unravaged.

540-49a. Makrin t' eisaphika<ne>: Macris was the ancient name of Scheria, named after the nurse of Dionysus. There, they say, Heracles came to be purified of the murder of his children, and married Melite, daughter of the river Aegaeus, from whom he had Hyllus; who, when he grew up, did not wish to be subject to Nausithous, but gathered the Phaeacians to the Cronian sea and settled them.
b. hyp' ophrysi: with knitted brows.
552-56a. alla, theai, pōs: the poet asks the Muse where the Argonauts sailed after the death of Apsyrtus and how they came to the sea.

Some criticize Apollonius for having said that Italy was called Ausonia at that time; for it was called so in later times than the Argonauts, from Auson, son of Odysseus and Calypso. But we shall say that since the poet himself named it so, even if it was not according to the times of those men.
b. nēsous te Ligystidas: near Italy there are three islands called Ligystiades, because they are inhabited by the Ligurians; and Stoechades because they are arranged in a row.
557. auton pou: after the inquiry, inspired, he begins the narrative from here.

564-66. hexeiēs plēthonto: the Liburnians, a people inhabiting these islands, Issa and Dysceladus and Pityeia; after which they came to Corcyra. He called the island called Pityussa Pityeia, following Homer (B 829).

577-80a. cholon ephrasath' Hērē: Hera, they say, knowing the wrath of Zeus against the Argonauts, made violent winds in those regions, so that they might depart from them and be carried to the Electrid island.
b. <tais autis: it is written> toi d' autis.
